title: To know what hurts
hookLine: Moshe Leib of Sassov learned love from a peasant: how can you love me if you don't know what hurts me?

cards: Love you. Love you too. How many times have you said it this month?
To a partner, a parent, a kid, a friend at the end of a phone call. It's a good habit. But here's a harder question.
Of the people you said it to, do you know what's hurting them right now? Not in general. This week.
Today's story is about a rebbe who said he learned what love means, not from a book, but from overhearing two men in a tavern.

teach.b: Moshe Leib of Sassov was a Hasidic rebbe in Galicia, remembered for his tenderness to the poor, the sick and the widowed. He used to say that he learned how to love people from a peasant.
He was at an inn where two villagers sat drinking. After a while, one turned to the other: tell me, do you love me?

teach.h: DO YOU LOVE ME? OF COURSE.
teach.b: The other said: of course I love you, with all my heart.
Then tell me, what hurts me? The second shrugged. How should I know what hurts you?
And the first said: if you don't know what hurts me, how can you say you love me? That's the whole story.
And Moshe Leib said: from that I understood that to love someone truly is to know their need, and to carry their sorrow with them. The Torah commands, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
It's easy to hear that as a feeling. The tavern turns it into a question of attention: you can't help carry someone's hurt if you've never asked what it is. There's humility in it, too.

The one who said of course I love you wasn't lying. He just hadn't looked. Moshe Leib's own life, as it's remembered, was one long answer: sitting with sick children, visiting widows, going where people hurt.

how: Moshe Leib of Sassov's tavern story is often told in Jewish teaching on the command to love one's neighbor, as a reminder that love means paying attention to another person's pain.

a peasant who asked his friend what hurt him

games.q: who said what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: of course, with all my heart

s: Moshe Leib said he learned love from a great book
he said he learned it from two villagers at an inn.
the second villager was lying when he said he loved his friend
he meant it. he just didn't know what hurt him.
Moshe Leib was remembered for caring for the sick and the widowed
his life, as it's remembered, answered the tavern's question.

games.q: your friend asks: do you love me? you say yes. then: what hurts me? you don't know. what now?
o: admit you don't know, and ask.
games.why: the villager's point: if you don't know what hurts me, how can you say you love me? love starts with asking.

practice: Bring to mind one person you love, and honestly ask: do I know what's hurting them right now?

If you do, hold it for a moment, as if carrying one corner of it; if you don't, think how you might ask them gently, without fixing anything: how are you, really? If you pray, pray for what hurts them.
